key_points_to_remember.text: `a / b` always returns a float (e.g., `4 / 2` results in `2.0`).
`//` is floor division: it returns the largest integer less than or equal to the result (e.g., `-5 // 2` is `-3`).
The modulo operator `%` follows the identity: `(a // b) * b + (a % b) == a`.
Exponentiation uses `**`; the `^` operator is bitwise XOR, not power.

lecture_snippets.explanation: x and y: True only if both True. x or y: False only if both False. not x: inverts. NOTE: && and || are Python operators but do something different (bitwise). Precedence: 'not' first, then 'and', then 'or'. Use parentheses to avoid confusion.

lecture_snippets.explanation: Precedence (high to low): comparisons → not → and → or. Use parentheses to be explicit. 'in' checks membership in sequence/set/dict-keys.

code_examples.code:

print(1 in [1,2,3])    # True
print(1 in (1,2,3))    # True
print('1' in '123')    # True (substring)
print(1 in {1:4, 2:3}) # True (checks keys)
print(4 in {1:4, 2:3}) # False (4 is value, not key)
print(1 in {1,2,3})    # True

lecture_snippets.explanation: A class is a blueprint. The __init__ method is the constructor called automatically when a new object is created to initialize attributes.

ai_summary.content: Merging joins two DataFrames based on a shared key column. The 'how' parameter determines the join type: 'inner' (intersection), 'outer' (union), 'left' (all from left), or 'right' (all from right). Missing matches result in NaN values.

key_points_to_remember.text: Default join: `.merge(df1, df2)` performs an `inner` join (only shared keys kept).
Missing data: `left`, `right`, and `outer` joins fill non-matching rows with `NaN`.
Different column names: Use `left_on='col_a', right_on='col_b'` if keys don't match exactly.
Duplicate columns: `suffixes=('_x', '_y')` handles non-key columns with the same name.
Join types: `left` keeps all left rows; `right` keeps all right; `outer` keeps all from both.
Index merging: Set `left_index=True` or `right_index=True` to join using the DataFrame index.

key_points_to_remember.text: Creation: `pd.Series(data, index=idx)`; if `index` is omitted, defaults to integer range `0..N`.
From Dictionary: `pd.Series({'A': 10, 'B': 20})` automatically sets keys as labels/index.
Data Alignment: Math operations between Series align by index label, not position; mismatches yield `NaN`.
Label vs Position: `s.loc['lab']` for explicit label; `s.iloc[0]` for integer position.

lecture_snippets.explanation: Selecting a single row/column with a label returns a Series; using a list/slice returns a DataFrame.

ai_summary.content: Selecting data in Pandas returns different types depending on the syntax used: a single label returns a Series, while a list of labels or a slice returns a DataFrame. Distinguishing between these is crucial for methods that only exist on one of the two types.

key_points_to_remember.text: Selection type: `df['col']` or `df.loc[label]` returns a Series (1D).
DataFrame forced: `df[['col']]` or `df.loc[[label]]` returns a DataFrame (2D).
Slicing rule: `df[0:1]` or `df.loc['A':'A']` returns a DataFrame, even for a single row.
Multi-column check: `df['A', 'B']` raises a KeyError; use a list `df[['A', 'B']]`.
Dimension check: `type(df.loc[0])` is Series; `type(df.loc[[0]])` is DataFrame.

ai_summary.content: .loc is used for label-based selection of rows and columns. A critical exam detail is that slicing with .loc is inclusive of the start AND the end label, unlike standard Python slicing.

key_points_to_remember.text: Label-based: `.loc` uses index/column names, not integer positions.
Inclusive slicing: `df.loc['A':'C']` includes both the start ('A') and end ('C') labels.
Format: `df.loc[row_labels, col_labels]` uses a comma to separate row and column selection.
Boolean indexing: `.loc` accepts boolean masks (e.g., `df.loc[df['A'] > 5]`).
Contrast: `.iloc` is exclusive of the end index and uses integer positions only.
Error check: `.loc` raises `KeyError` if a specified label is not found in the index.

lecture_snippets.explanation: Label-based selection. Slicing with .loc is inclusive of the end name.

lecture_snippets.explanation: Integer-position based selection. Slicing with .iloc is exclusive of the end index (like standard Python lists).

code_examples.code: df.iloc[0:2, 0:1] # Rows 0,1; Col 0

lecture_snippets.question: What happens if you run print(df.iloc[5, 2]) on a DataFrame with only 3 rows?

options.a: It returns None

options.c: It raises an IndexError

key_points_to_remember.text: Position-based: `.iloc` uses 0-based integer offsets only.
Exclusive slicing: `df.iloc[0:2]` returns rows 0 and 1 (index 2 is excluded).

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [3, 1, 2]})
# ERROR: sort_values requires the 'by' argument
df.sort_values(ascending=False)
ai_examples.why: You must tell Pandas which column(s) to use for the value comparison.

ai_examples.title: Assuming In-place Change
ai_examples.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'X': [5, 2, 9]})
df.sort_values(by='X')
# Trap: df is still [5, 2, 9] here
print(df.iloc[0])
ai_examples.why: Pandas methods usually return a new DataFrame. You must re-assign: df = df.sort_values(...).

key_points_to_remember.text: df.sort_values(by='col', ascending=True): 'by' is required; 'ascending' defaults to True.
df.sort_index(axis=0): sorts by row labels; axis=1 sorts by column labels (names).
Multi-column sort: df.sort_values(by=['A', 'B']) handles primary and secondary sorting.
Inplace check: .sort_values() returns a new object unless inplace=True is specified.
Missing data: NaN values are placed at the end by default (na_position='last').

lecture_snippets.explanation: datetime.now() retrieves the current local time. timestamp() returns the seconds since the Unix Epoch (Jan 1, 1970).

code_examples.code:
from datetime import datetime
print(datetime.now().timestamp())

ai_summary.content: The datetime module provides tools for current time retrieval. .now() returns a datetime object, while .timestamp() converts that object into a float representing seconds since the Unix Epoch (Jan 1, 1970).

bullets: What is the data type of the value returned by .timestamp()?
What date/time is the Unix Epoch?
How to get the current year from a datetime object?
Difference between datetime.now() and datetime.today().
Importing: from datetime import datetime vs import datetime.

ai_examples.title: Get Current Timestamp
ai_examples.code:
from datetime import datetime
now = datetime.now()
# Returns float (seconds since 1970)
ts = now.timestamp()
print(type(ts))
ai_examples.why: Correct way to get the numeric Unix representation of current time.

ai_examples.title: Extracting Components
ai_examples.code:
from datetime import datetime
dt = datetime.now()
print(f"Year: {dt.year}, Month: {dt.month}")
ai_examples.why: Datetime objects have attributes like .year, .month, .day, .hour etc.

ai_examples.title: Calling timestamp on Module
ai_examples.code:
import datetime
# ERROR: timestamp() is a method of a datetime instance
ts = datetime.timestamp()
ai_examples.why: You must first create an instance (like datetime.datetime.now()) before calling .timestamp().

ai_examples.title: Wrong Unix Epoch Date
ai_examples.code:
# Common trap: Thinking epoch is 1900 or 2000
# Epoch is Jan 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC.
ai_examples.why: 1970 is the standard reference point for almost all modern computing timestamps.

key_points_to_remember.text: Import trap: 'from datetime import datetime' -> datetime.now(); 'import datetime' -> datetime.datetime.now().
dt.timestamp(): returns a float representing seconds since the Unix Epoch (Jan 1, 1970).
datetime.fromtimestamp(ts): converts a float/int timestamp back into a local datetime object.
Component access: .year, .month, .day, .hour return integers (attributes, not methods).
datetime.now() vs .today(): now() allows a timezone (tz) argument; today() is always local.

lecture_snippets.explanation: Objects that can be traversed using next(). Lists can be turned into iterators using iter(). They raise StopIteration when exhausted.

code_examples.code: it = iter([1, 2]); print(next(it)); print(next(it))

ai_summary.content: Iterators are objects that yield values one at a time via the next() function. Once all items are yielded, the iterator raises StopIteration. Any iterable (like a list) can be converted to an iterator using iter().

bullets: What exception is raised when an iterator is empty?
Can you reuse an iterator once it has finished?
Difference between an iterable (list) and an iterator.
How does a for-loop handle StopIteration internally?
Using next() with a default value to avoid exceptions.

ai_examples.title: Manual Iteration
ai_examples.code:
nums = [10, 20]
it = iter(nums)
print(next(it)) # 10
print(next(it)) # 20
ai_examples.why: iter() creates the iterator, and next() retrieves the next available element.

ai_examples.title: Handling Exhaustion
ai_examples.why: StopIteration is the standard way Python signals the end of a sequence.

ai_examples.title: next() on a List
ai_examples.code:
lst = [1, 2, 3]
# ERROR: list is not an iterator
print(next(lst))
ai_examples.why: You must call iter(lst) first to create an iterator object from the list.

ai_examples.title: Double Iteration Trap
ai_examples.code:
it = iter([1, 2])
list(it) # Consumes the iterator
# This next() will raise StopIteration immediately
print(next(it))
ai_examples.why: Iterators are 'one-way'. Once you consume them (via list(), for-loops, etc.), they are empty.

key_points_to_remember.text: Creation: it = iter(iterable) turns a list, string, or tuple into a stateful iterator.
Consumption: next(it) retrieves the next item or raises StopIteration if empty.
Safe retrieval: next(it, default_value) returns the default instead of raising an exception.
One-way traversal: Iterators are 'spent' after use and cannot be reset or reused.
Internal loop logic: For-loops call iter() and catch StopIteration automatically.
